name: Marco Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the small electric company that covers our town and the valley around it, about forty people all told. My dad was a lineman there for thirty-one years, so half the old guys knew me as a kid. A normal day, we load the truck at seven, go out and change a pole or fix a service line to some farmhouse, and I do whatever the journeyman tells me, mostly digging, hauling and holding the ladder.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work and people in town see you doing it. What wears me out is how much I still don't know. I'm slow with the theory, the formulas and the books, I'm better with my hands, and the journeymen have to explain things twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Around here nobody believed it in the first place. I'd say it at the diner or after church, I don't go online for that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay the way they ought to be. People do the work, people get paid for it. A computer can't hold a pole steady in the wind, and that's the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, finish my apprenticeship, keep the money I've got put away, which is a few months' worth. Maybe help my uncle fix up the roof on the house I rent from him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like things are as they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody around here believed it. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we've heard it all before. When I was nineteen, the sawmill here got told new machines would make it more competitive, and two years later it closed anyway because a bigger automated mill opened four hours away. People here don't trust promises from far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did you work at the sawmill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, straight out of school. It was a good job until it wasn't. That's why I went into lines, you can't ship a power line to another town.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because nobody around here believed it in the first place. I'd say it at the diner or after church, not online.
S0.think: It means things stay the way they ought to be: people do the work and get paid for it. A computer can't hold a pole steady in the wind.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, finishing his apprenticeship and keeping his savings of a few months. Helps his uncle repair the roof on the house he rents from him.
S0.feel: Calm, as if things are as they should be.
S0.quote: A computer can't hold a pole steady in the wind, and that's the end of it.
S0.fieldNote: Marco's distrust of technology isn't abstract: he lost his first job when a sawmill closed after an automated rival opened. He chose line work specifically because it can't be moved elsewhere. His sense of the right order of things, people working and being paid, runs through everything he says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and adapt, same as always. But I'd also say I don't want some company from the city deciding how we do things here. At church I'd keep it to small talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd say. I saw what new machines did to the sawmill, and I don't want to go through that twice before I'm thirty. I'm not good with the computer side, and if that's what they start judging us on, I'm in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and try to finish my apprenticeship early so I've at least got the ticket. I'd save harder, maybe put my truck payment towards savings once it's paid off next spring. I wouldn't go looking for computer courses, I'd do what the company makes me do and no more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the feeling before the sawmill news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say keep your head down, work hard and they'll keep you. That's how it worked for him. I'm not sure it works like that anymore, but I wouldn't tell him that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do what the company makes you do and no more. What if that's not enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to think again, I suppose. But I'd rather be the guy they can count on in a storm than the guy who's good on a tablet. I'd hope that still counts for something.

S1.say: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and adapt, same as always. But I don't want a company from the city deciding how we do things here.
S1.think: It worries me more than I'd say, because I saw what new machines did to the sawmill. I'm not good with computers, and if that's what they judge us on, I'm in trouble.
S1.do: Keeps working and tries to finish his apprenticeship early to secure the ticket. Moves his truck payment into savings once the truck is paid off next spring and does only the training the company requires.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the feeling before the sawmill closed.
S1.quote: I'm not good with the computer side, and if that's what they start judging us on, I'm in trouble.
S1.fieldNote: His public line about self-reliance sits next to a private fear rooted in the sawmill closure. He'd keep his father's advice to work hard and stay put, while privately doubting it still holds. His only lever is to be dependable in a storm rather than good with a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and the big tech companies don't care who they wreck. I wouldn't say the government should hand everyone money, I don't believe in that. I'd say families and towns are going to have to look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be in a bad spot. Two years, I won't even have my ticket, and I've got no other skills a robot can't do. I already lost one job to a machine I never saw. I'd be losing the second one before I've learned it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any spending that isn't needed, no new rifle, no trips, nothing. I'd keep working as long as they'd have me and ask my uncle about working with him on the side, he does plumbing. I'd lean on family and church, that's what they're for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick in the stomach, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know if I'd say anything. He'd see it on the news and we'd sit on the porch and not talk about it. In my family that's how you talk about bad things, you sit there and you don't talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want government handouts. If it came to that, would you take help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take help from family first, then church. Government only if I really had nothing. I'd hate it, but I'm not stupid, I wouldn't let myself go hungry over pride.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong and the big tech companies don't care who they wreck. I don't believe in government handing out money, so families and towns will have to look after their own.
S2.think: I'd be in a bad spot, without my ticket and with no skills a robot can't do. I already lost one job to a machine I never saw and would lose this one before I've learned it properly.
S2.do: Stops all non-essential spending straight away and keeps working as long as he's kept on. Asks his uncle about plumbing work on the side and leans on family and church.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick to his stomach.
S2.quote: I already lost one job to a machine I never saw. I'd be losing the second one before I've learned it properly.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture would mean a second job lost to machines before he's thirty, and he says so plainly. He blames big tech but rejects government handouts, ranking family, then church, then state. The porch scene with his father shows a family that copes in silence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so people should get to work and not wait for anyone to save them. I'd say the company should train its own people first before bringing in machines. That's how it should be, apprentices learning from the older guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd have my ticket, at least. I'd be a lineman like my dad, for a few years. But I'd know it was ending, and that's a hard thing to carry around every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship and work every hour I can to build the savings past six months. I'd start helping my uncle on plumbing jobs on weekends so I've got something else in my hands. I'd wait and see how fast the robots actually come before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's better than the two years, but it sits on you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help your uncle with plumbing. Wouldn't robots do plumbing too, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. But it's family work, and family looks after each other. If my uncle's still working, he'll find me something to do, robot or no robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act on something bigger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the company buy one of those machines. We're a small company, so if even we buy one, then everyone has. That would be the sign.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a few years, so people should get to work and not wait to be saved. The company should train its own people before bringing in machines.
S3.think: Five years means I'd get my ticket and be a lineman like my dad for a few years. But I'd know it was ending, and that's hard to carry every day.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and works every hour possible to build savings past six months. Starts helping his uncle on plumbing jobs at weekends and waits to see how fast robots arrive.
S3.feel: Anxious, better than two years but weighing on him.
S3.quote: If my uncle's still working, he'll find me something to do, robot or no robot.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets him follow his father into the trade, but with the end in sight. His fallback is family loyalty more than a new skill, and he admits plumbing may not be safe either. He'd treat his own small company buying a robot as the signal to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for people to get ready on their own, without the government telling them how. I'd say get a trade, buy some land if you can, look after your family. That's what I'd say after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is better, but I don't trust that anyone's going to look after people like me at the end of it. So I'd want to need less from anyone. Land, a woodstove and a freezer full of deer meat. That's my retirement plan if the robots win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship and work as a lineman for as long as it lasts. In the first few years I'd save for a deposit on a few acres my uncle has been talking about selling. I'd keep saving and not do anything with computers unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but steadier. I'd have something to work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the ten years change any plans about family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to get married someday and have kids, that's always been the plan. It'd make me want a woman who's practical, who can live simple. My mum would say I'm making it a requirement for the wrong reasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do anything with computers unless you had to. Even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with ten years. I'm not going to spend a decade learning to be second best at something a machine will do better anyway. I'd rather be first-rate at what I'm already doing.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for people to get ready without the government telling them how. Get a trade, buy some land if you can and look after your family.
S4.think: Ten years is better, but I don't trust anyone to look after people like me at the end, so I'd want to need less from anyone. Land, a woodstove and a freezer of deer meat is my plan.
S4.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and works as a lineman as long as it lasts. Saves for a deposit on a few acres his uncle may sell and avoids computers unless required.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but steadier with something to work towards.
S4.quote: Land, a woodstove and a freezer full of deer meat. That's my retirement plan if the robots win.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Marco's answer is self-reliance: land, wood heat and hunting rather than retraining. He flatly refuses to spend the time learning computers, seeing no point in being second best to a machine. Even his marriage hopes bend towards a simpler life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd lose my second job to machines before I'm thirty. What would help is companies having to keep and train their own people first, apprentices especially, instead of throwing them out the second a machine shows up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it does to a town. When the sawmill closed, the hardware store went, then the bakery, then half the church. If the robots do every job, I don't know what holds a place like ours together.

headlineQuote: I'm not going to spend a decade learning to be second best at something a machine will do better anyway.
portrait: Marco is a 27-year-old second-year apprentice at the small electric company where his father worked for thirty-one years, better with his hands than with the books. He lost his first job when the local sawmill closed after an automated rival opened, and that memory shapes how he sees every scenario. He doesn't use AI and won't, trusting family and church over government. He's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy about steady disruption and alarmed by the two-year AGI picture, where he'd lose a second job before thirty. With more time he'd become a lineman like his father and plan for self-reliance on a few acres rather than retrain.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he would lose a second job to machines before he turns thirty.
whatWouldHelp: Companies being required to keep and train their own people first, apprentices especially, instead of dropping them when a machine arrives.
